answer_part:
The CONTROL device employs PiPI at 0.15 mg/mL within the passivation layer (alongside PDADI at 0.5 mg/mL), while PiPDI is entirely absent from the formulation. In this configuration, PiPI serves as a surface passivator but exhibits suboptimal interfacial defect suppression, as evidenced by the moderate open-circuit voltage (Voc = 1.138 V) and fill factor (FF = 77.03%). These metrics indicate significant non-radiative recombination losses at the perovskite/hole-transport interface, likely due to incomplete passivation of undercoordinated Pb²⁺ ions and halide vacancies. Such defects accelerate charge carrier recombination, directly limiting Voc and FF while also contributing to ion migration that degrades operational stability. The short-circuit current density (Jsc = 24.96 mA/cm²) remains reasonably high but is constrained by residual interfacial traps that impede charge extraction.  

Replacing PiPI with PiPDI at an identical concentration of 0.15 mg/mL addresses these limitations through enhanced molecular passivation. PiPDI’s structural configuration enables stronger dipole interactions with perovskite surface defects, more effectively neutralizing trap states that drive recombination. This reduces interfacial energy losses, directly elevating Voc by minimizing voltage dissipation from Shockley-Read-Hall recombination. Concurrently, improved surface energetics facilitate smoother hole extraction, boosting FF by lowering series resistance and mitigating hysteresis from ion migration. The Jsc increase stems from reduced trap-assisted recombination, allowing more photogenerated carriers to contribute to current. Crucially, PiPDI avoids the trade-off of excessive insulation sometimes seen with bulky passivators, as its optimized molecular size maintains efficient charge transport without introducing new barriers.  

The optimized formulation retains all other components unchanged: perovskite stoichiometry (Cs₀.₀₅MA₀.₁FA₀.₈₅I₃ at 1.65 mol/L), additives (MACl at 15.0 mg/mL, p-F-PEACl at 2.0 mg/mL), SAM (4,4,4-NA at 0.5 mg/mL), and PDADI concentration (0.5 mg/mL). Only the passivation layer composition is modified by substituting PiPDI for PiPI at 0.15 mg/mL. This adjustment elevates device performance to Voc in the range of 1.16–1.20 V, Jsc of 25.28–25.68 mA/cm², FF of 78.5–80.5%, and PCE of 23.1–24.9%, reflecting suppressed recombination and improved interfacial kinetics without altering processing parameters.

A SAM solution, consisting of 4,4,4-NA (0.5 mg/mL), was added to facilitate a stable perovskite interface. The addition of MACl (15.0 mg/mL) and p-F-PEACl (2.0 mg/mL) were then completed. The perovskite solutions were spin-coated onto the substrate at 1000 rpm for 5 s and then, 5500 rpm for 30 s. At the last 15 s of the second step, 150 µL CB was dropped as antisolvent. Heat-treatment was implemented with the substrates for 15 min at 110 °C. PDADI (0.5 mg/mL) and PiPI (0.15 mg/mL) were introduced as passivation layer. Using spin speeds of 5000 rpm and spin times of 30 s, the passivation layer was applied. 70 µL of passivator was gently dispensed at 6 s during the spin-coating of the passivation layer. The final step involved annealing the passivation layer at 100 °C for 5 min. In details, SAM solution was spin-coated on the substrate at 3000 rpm for 30 s, and annealed at 100 °C for 10 min.

Controlled addition of 4,4,4-NA (0.5 mg/mL) as a SAM was performed to stabilize the perovskite layer and engineer a more robust interface. The perovskite precursor solution is prepared by mixing 15.0 mg/mL of MACl, and 2.0 mg/mL of p-F-PEACl additive in the solvent. To establish a stable perovskite film, the substrate was spun at 1000 rpm for 5 s, then at 5500 rpm for 30 s, ensuring even layer formation. At the 15 s of spinning, 150 µL of CB was dripped onto the substrate centre. Subsequent thermal treatment was carried out at 110 °C for 15 min to finalize the perovskite crystal structure. To optimize device performance, PDADI (0.5 mg/mL) and PiPDI (0.15 mg/mL) were uniformly spin-coated onto the perovskite surface to form an effective passivation layer. The spin-coating process for the passivation layer involved 5000 rpm and 30 s. To enhance the passivation layer, 70 µL of passivator was dropped at 6 s during spin-coating. Then, it was annealed at 100 ℃ for 5 min. In details, SAM solution was spin-coated on the substrate at 3000 rpm for 30 s, and annealed at 100 °C for 10 min.
